results.question: Show top 5 employees by salary
results.expected_sql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5
results.generated_sql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5
results.note: Exact match — model produces identical SQL

results.question: Show top 5 employees by salary
results.expected_sql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5
results.generated_sql: SELECT e.name, e.salary FROM employees e ORDER BY e.salary DESC LIMIT 5
results.note: Alias variation — semantically equivalent, not exact match

results.question: Total sales revenue by region
results.expected_sql: SELECT c.region, SUM(s.total_amount) as revenue FROM sales s JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.region
results.generated_sql: SELECT c.region, SUM(s.total_amount) AS total_revenue FROM sales s INNER JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.region ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
results.note: Structural equivalent — different alias, extra ORDER BY, INNER vs implicit JOIN

results.question: Which department has the highest average salary?
results.expected_sql: SELECT d.name, AVG(e.salary) as avg_salary FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id GROUP BY d.name ORDER BY avg_salary DESC LIMIT 1
results.generated_sql: SELECT d.name, AVG(e.salary) as avg_salary FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id GROUP BY d.name ORDER BY avg_salary DESC LIMIT 1

results.question: How many employees are in each department?
results.expected_sql: SELECT d.name as department, COUNT(e.id) as employee_count FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id GROUP BY d.name
results.generated_sql: SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id GROUP BY d.name
results.note: Different join direction, COUNT(*) vs COUNT(e.id), different alias

results.question: Show products with low stock
results.expected_sql: SELECT name, stock_quantity FROM products WHERE stock_quantity < 100 ORDER BY stock_quantity ASC
results.generated_sql: SELECT name, stock_quantity FROM products WHERE stock_quantity < 50 ORDER BY stock_quantity
results.note: Threshold difference — model chose 50 instead of 100

results.question: What is the total sales revenue?
results.expected_sql: SELECT SUM(total_amount) as total_revenue FROM sales
results.generated_sql: SELECT SUM(total_amount) as total_revenue FROM sales

results.question: Find products that have never been sold
results.expected_sql: SELECT p.name, p.category, p.price FROM products p LEFT JOIN sales s ON p.id = s.product_id WHERE s.sale_id IS NULL
results.generated_sql: SELECT p.name, p.category, p.price FROM products p WHERE p.id NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM sales)
results.note: Different approach (NOT IN subquery vs LEFT JOIN IS NULL) — structurally different but semantically equivalent

results.question: Show the running total of sales by date
results.expected_sql: SELECT sale_date, SUM(total_amount) as daily_total, SUM(SUM(total_amount)) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) as running_total FROM sales GROUP BY sale_date ORDER BY sale_date
results.generated_sql: SELECT sale_date, total_amount, SUM(total_amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) as running_total FROM sales ORDER BY sale_date
results.note: Window function variation — different granularity (per-row vs per-day)

results.question: Compare sales between North America and Europe
results.expected_sql: SELECT c.region, COUNT(s.sale_id) as num_sales, SUM(s.total_amount) as total_revenue FROM sales s JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.region IN ('North America', 'Europe') GROUP BY c.region
results.generated_sql: SELECT c.region, COUNT(*) as sale_count, SUM(s.total_amount) as revenue FROM sales s JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.region IN ('North America', 'Europe') GROUP BY c.region
results.note: Minor variation — COUNT(*) vs COUNT(s.sale_id), different alias
